[ 21 ] Switching to other solvents with high dielectric constant such as dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) or dimethylacetamide (DMA) facilitates the production of sulfur radicals and the full utilization of the sulfur, but the cycling stability of the cell is also sacrifi ced and the unstable interface between the reactive DMSO/DMA solvent and Li metal raises other concerns.

[ 22,23 ] Alternative cell designs incorporating solid-state electrolytes completely prevent the dissolution of polysulfi des, but the utilization of the sulfur (i.e., the reversible capacity) is also largely reduced.
[ 24 ] Therefore, the solubility of the polysulfi des in cells with liquid electrolytes needs to be carefully tuned and well understood.
In most studies, a low sulfur loading (less than 1 mg cm –2 ) is used, but a high S loading is desired for high-capacity full cells.
[ 25,26 ] In this paper, lithium trifl uoromethyl-4,5-dicyanoimidazole (LiTDI) is studied for Li-S cells.
We study the effect of LiTDI on the solubility of polysulfi des.
The performance of this electrolyte was investigated with a high sulfur (i.e., practically usable) loading at 3 mg cm –2 under a high current density.
A comparison of the physical properties of electrolytes with either 1 M LiTFSI or LiTDI in DOL/DME (1/1, v/v) is shown in Table 1 .
Both electrolytes have a comparable conductivity and viscosity, suitable for the electrochemical needs, but an 83% decrease in the Li 2 S 8 solubility is observed in the LiTDI electrolyte.

Restricting the polysulfi de solubility to a low level is expected to improve the Li-S cell cycle life because of the suppression of the polysulfi de shuttle mechanism, reduction of anode contamination, and the minimization of the loss of active material from the cathode.

[ 22 ] To understand the relationship between the polysulfi de solubility and electrolyte supporting salt, 7 Li and 17 O nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopic measurements were used to aid in understanding the solvation interactions.
The δ ( 7 Li) for the LiTDI and LiTFSI-based electrolytes without polysulfi des was –0.8 and –1.2 ppm (relative to Li + cations fully solvated by H 2 O molecules) ( Figure 1 a–c), respectively.
The δ ( 17 O) for the DME molecules shifts to ≈ –27.7 and –26.9 ppm in the LiTDI and LiTFSI-based electrolytes, respectively, from –24.3 ppm in a neat DOL/DME solvent mixture.
The δ ( 17 O) for the DOL molecules near 35 ppm shifts by 1–2 ppm.

The smaller shift of δ ( 17 O) for the DOL molecules relative to the DME molecules and signifi cant broadening of the peaks for the latter suggest that the Li + cations may be preferentially solvated by the DME.

[ 27 ] It has been reported that the solvation of Li + cations in the electrolyte affects the short-chain polysulfi de solubility by solvating the Li + ion in the polysulfi des, but it did not affect the Lithium-sulfur (Li-S) batteries have attracted wide interest due to their potential high capacity (1672 mAh g −1 ), low environmental impact, and low cost.
The commercialization of Li-S batteries is hindered, however, by capacity fading upon extensive cycling.
This is principally caused by the dissolution of the lithium polysulfi des generated during the discharge/charge reactions.
[ 1,2 ] The soluble polysulfi des easily migrate out of the cathode and diffuse into the electrolyte.

The “corrosive” electrolyte containing polysulfi des continuously reacts with the Li metal anode (the so-called shuttle mechanism), thereby increasing the cell impedance by forming an insulating layer on the anode.
All these factors contribute to the poor cycling stability and low round-trip effi ciency of Li-S batteries.

[ 3 ] A general approach to address the capacity fading issue is to confi ne the soluble polysulfi de species in carbon scaffolds (the sulfur active material is an insulator so the carbon also serves as to the electron conductor for the sulfur) with various architectures including porous carbons, carbon nanotubes, and graphene.
[ 4–9 ] The functionalization of carbon substrate or the direct incorporation of oxides such as metal-organic frameworks further immobilizes the polysulfi de anions at the atomic level.
[ 10–13 ] Different polymers have also been studied to stabilize the polysulfi des through the formation of chemical bonds with the sulfur.

[ 14–16 ] In contrast, reducing the polysulfi de solubility by modifying the electrolyte formulation has been less explored, possibly due to the complicated interactions between the ions, solvent molecules, and polysulfi des during the electrochemical processes.

[ 17,18 ] The state-of-the-art electrolyte formulation used for Li-ion batteries (e.g., LiPF 6 in an ethylene carbonate/dimethyl carbonate (or other acyclic carbonate) solvent mixture) is not suitable for Li-S cells due to the incompatibility between the carbonate solvents and the polysulfi des and S 3 · radicals.
[ 19,20 ] The most widely used electrolyte for Li-S cells therefore is Adv.

[ 21,22 ] To further understand the polysulfi de chemistry, the temperature-dependent diffusion coeffi cients were measured by various temperature NMR methods.
The results in Figure S1 (Supporting Information) show that these coeffi cients were well aligned with the Stokes– Einstein theory of diffusion.

The variation of hydrodynamic radius of Li + cation, r s,Li / r Li for these electrolytes before and after adding 0.05 M Li 2 S 8 was calculated on the basis of diffusion coeffi cients of the DOL solvent since Li + ion did not have much coordination effects on DOL from 17 O NMR spectra.
The hydrodynamic radius of Li + cation in both the electrolytes is close to each other before adding the lithium polysulfi des.
After adding the additive, the radius of the solvated cation in the LiTFSI-based electrolyte remains the same.
However, in the LiTDI-based electrolyte, it increased by 20% (Table S1 of the Supporting Information).
This suggests that the sizes of lithium polysulfi de agglomerates in solution are larger in the LiTDI-based electrolyte.
To explain the Li + ion solvation with polysulfi des, ab initio molecular dynamics (AI-MD) simulation was performed on Li 2 S 8 in the electrolyte (Figure 1 d,e).

AI-MD simulation reveals that the solvated Li 2 S 8 species in different Li-salt electrolytes at same concentration yields different subsequent lithium polysulfi de species under equilibration at T = 300 K.
This could be due to the different Li + solvation level in the electrolyte and the different anion interaction.
For the LiTDI electrolyte, two Li 2 S 4 were formed, whereas for the LiTFSI electrolyte, the Li 2 S 3 and Li 2 S 5 were generated.

The two Li 2 S 4 species in LiTDI solution tend to agglomerate into a dimer with Li 4 S 8 -like cluster, in contrast to the separation of Li 2 S 3 and Li 2 S 5 in LiTFSI solutions as observed in previous studies.
[ 28 ] The radius of the Li 4 S 8 dimer is much larger than that of the separated Li 2 S 4 , which is well aligned with the hydrodynamic radius observation in the NMR studies.
TDI anion contains more reactive nitrogen-containing functional group like nitrile and imide, which has been proven to affect the polysulfi de stability in the carbon host.
[ 10 ] It should be noted that the chemical synthesized Li 2 S 8 solution in the experiment is a complex mixture of different state polysulfi des, including Li 2 S 6 and S 3 − radicals.

[ 20,23 ] However, with the same simulation conditions and the Density functional theory (DFT) calculations of Gibbs energy, the favorable species in different electrolytes were determined with reaction a and reaction b shown in Figure S3 (Supporting Information), respectively.

This case indicates that supporting salts would affect the chemical reduction reaction of long-chain polysulfi de (i.e., Li 2 S 8 ) and result in a manageable optimization of the polysulfi de solubility.
Figure 2 a shows the fi rst cycle charge– discharge behavior of cells with these two electrolytes.

In order to obtain a reproducible result from the batch-to-batch study, the sulfur to electrolyte ratio (S/E) needs to be optimized fi rst for each formulation, as shown in Figure S2 (Supporting Information).
[ 29,30 ] The initial capacity is lower for the cell with the LiTDI electrolyte than that for the cell with the LiTFSI electrolyte (995 vs 1170 mAh g −1 ).
This lower sulfur utilization with the LiTDI-based electrolyte may be attributed to the low solubility of the Adv.

[ 31 ] No obvious overpotential is observed, which indicates the extensive penetration of the LiTDI electrolyte into the carbon cathode.

When sulfur to electrolyte ratio is increased from 50 g S /L E to 70 g S /L E in the cell using LiTDI electrolyte, a higher Coulombic effi ciency (CE) and slower capacity decay are obtained (Figure 2 b).
Both the reduced amount of the electrolyte per cell and the reduced polysulfi de solubility would decrease the capacity loss by suppressing sulfur loss (Figure S2 of the Supporting Information).
[ 29 ] After 100 cycles, the capacity retention is 25% higher with the LiTDI electrolyte than for the LiTFSI electrolyte.

In addition, the initial CE of the Li-S cell with the LiTDI electrolyte is much improved (Figure 2 b) due to the reduction in the shuttle mechanism, in sharp contrast to the LiTFSI cell for which the polysulfi de shuttle is quite evident (Figure 2 a).
[ 32 ] One of the most critical issues for the practical utilization of Li-S batteries is to increase the cell performance with a high sulfur loading.
Cathode wettability becomes a critical challenge as the sulfur loading increases.
Another challenge associated with such cathodes is that rapid Li anode degradation occurs for cycled cells with a high areal capacity (AC).
[ 33,34 ] Figure 3 compares the charge–discharge curves and cycling performance of a cell with 3 mg S cm −2 loading.
The cell is fi rst discharged/ charged at a C/10 (i.e., 10 h) rate (0.5 mA cm −2 ) for 5 cycles, followed by a C/2 (i.e., 2 h) rate (2.4 mA cm −2 ) up to 300 cycles.
Both of the cells with the 1 M LiTFSI or LiTDI in DOL/DME electrolytes have only a 300 mAh g −1 discharge capacity due to the large polarization for the thick sulfur cathode.

The polysulfi de additives will promote the polysulfi de dissolution to an equilibrium state and the EIS spectrum of the cell would be greatly reduced so that it would not only promote the electrode initial capacity delivery but also help in the capacity retention.
[ 35,36 ] However, after adding polysulfi des, LiNO 3 is needed to prevent the shuttle problem toward the anode side.

In this study, only 40 × 10 –3 M Li 2 S 8 (which is only 1% comparing to the sulfur in the cathode) and 0.2 M LiNO 3 were added to the electrolytes and the polysulfi de additive itself does not contribute to the calculation of the total capacity.

For the cells with the electrolytes containing the additives, the sulfur cathodes were well wetted in both the LiTFSI and LiTDI-based electrolytes and both the cells achieved a high initial capacity of 1140 and 1110 mAh g −1 , respectively.

In addition, the increased amount of polysulfi des in the LiTFSI-based electrolyte accelerated the failure of the Li metal anode.
Therefore, the CE dropped to ≈80% and the capacity decayed quickly after 150 cycles.
In contrast, the cell with the LiTDI-based electrolyte showed stable cycling at 570 mAh g −1 for 300 cycles.
Because of the relatively low concentration of polysulfi de in the electrolyte, the LiNO 3 consumption was greatly decreased as can be seen from the high and stable CE (99%).

The reduced dissolution of polysulfi de from the cathode scaffold together with the additive polysulfi de penetration helped a full delivery under the thick electrode condition and stabilized the electrode during the cycling.
As a result, the cell using LiTDI as a supporting salt with LiNO 3 and polysulfi de additive reached a 1.67 mAh cm −2 areal capacity after 300 stable cycles.

[ 3 ] In contrast, the Li metal anode in the cell with the LiTDI-based electrolyte had a dense deposition structure for both the surface and cross sections (Figure 4 b).

In addition, scanning electron microscope (SEM) and Electron-dispersive X-ray spectrum (EDX) analyses of the cycled cathode (Figure 4 d) in LiTDI-based cell show a 54% sulfur retention in the cathode, which is twice as high as that for the LiTFSI-based electrolyte (Figure 4 c).
Therefore, the use of the LiTDI salt suppressed the shuttle mechanism effi - ciently and stabilized the electrolyte interface with both cathode and anode.

In conclusion, the use of LiTDI as a supporting electrolyte salt for Li-S batteries effectively decreases the polysulfi de solubility thereby minimizing the polysulfi de shuttle mechanism (i.e., which causes a loss of active sulfur material from the cathode and the degradation of the Li metal anode).
NMR and DFT calculation indicated a higher Li + solvation mainly with the DME in the DOL/DME mixture, which is different in the dilute solution from that of the concentrated pure DME solution.
AIMD simulation reveals that the TDI anion coordination affects the polysulfi de disproportion to form Li 4 S 8 dimer and reduced the solubility.

Furthermore, with the incorporation of 0.1% Li 2 S 8 and 0.2 M LiNO 3 additives, excellent Li–S cell performance with cathodes having a high sulfur (3 mg S cm −2 ) loading was obtained using the LiTDI-based electrolyte.
Experimental Section The procedure to prepare S-coated multi-walled carbon nanotubes (S-CNT) was previously reported.
[ 37 ] Elemental sulfur (S 8 , Alfa Aesar) and the MWCNTs (Cheap Tubes Inc.) (80:20 w/w) were mixed together by mechanical ball milling for 5 h.
The mixture was then sealed in a polytetrafl uoroethylene (PTFE) container and heated to 155 °C in an oven for 24 h under the protection of inert Ar gas.
Morphology observations were performed with a dual-focus ion beam (FIB) SEM (FEI Helios).

The 7 Li and 17 O NMR spectra for these electrolytes were obtained from Fourier transformed free induction decays after a single pulse excitation at Larmor frequencies of 233.2 and 81.4 MHz, respectively, at ambient temperature (≈25 °C) using a 600 MHz NMR spectrometer (Agilent, USA) equipped with a 5 mm liquid NMR probe (Doty Scientifi c, USA).
The 7 Li and 17 O chemical shifts for a 1 M LiCl in H 2 O solution and dilute water were used as external references (i.e., 0 ppm), respectively.
The ionic conductivity of the electrolytes was measured by a conductivity meter (Orion 3 Star, Thermo Scientifi c) at 30 °C.
The shear viscosity ( η ) of the electrolytes was measured using a viscometer (Brookfi eld, DV2T) at 30 °C.
All of the measurements were performed more than twice to ensure their reliability.

Calculation of the Variation of Hydrodynamic Radius, r s , Li /r Li : The temperature-dependent diffusion coeffi cients measured for LiTFSI and LITDI-based electrolytes plotted in Figure S1 (Supporting Information) were in well agreement with the Stokes–Einstein theory of diffusion, D = k B T /6π ηr s , where k B , T , η , and r s are the Boltzmann constant, absolute temperature, viscosity, and hydrodynamic radius of diffusing molecules, respectively.

Based on the variations of diffusion coeffi cient and δ ( 17 O) of solvent molecules, the interaction of DOL molecules to other electrolyte components was assumed negligible than the hydrodynamic radius of DOL molecules; ( r s,DOL ) will be the same to its actual size for all samples, r s,DOL = r DOL .

And if both Li + and DOL were completely isolated from other components of the electrolyte, the diffusion ratio D 0,Li / D 0,DOL = r DOL / r Li , where D 0,Li and D 0,DOL were the diffusion coeffi cients of Li + and DOL without any interaction to other electrolyte components and r DOL and r Li were the sizes of DOL and Li + cation.
Therefore, the variations of hydrodynamic radius of Li + cation were as follow: ( D 0,Li / D 0,DOL )/( D Li / D DOL ) = ( r DOL / r Li )/( r s , DOL / r s , Li ) = r s , Li / r Li .
This value was proportional to the degree of ion association between Li + cations and anions.
Using the diffusion coeffi cients the ratio r s,Li / r Li for LiTFSI and LiTDI-based electrolytes was calculated with and without 0.05 M Li 2 S 8 .
The larger value of r s,Li / r Li refl ected the larger size of Li complexes.

Electrochemical Measurements : The thin cathode with <1 mg S cm −2 loading was prepared by mixing 80 wt% S-CNT composite powder, 10 wt% Super P (Timcal Graphite & Carbon), and 10 wt% polyvinylidene fl uoride (PVDF) binder together and adding N -methyl-2-pyrrolidinone to form a slurry.
The slurry was then coated onto an Al foil current collector and dried at 60 °C under vacuum overnight.

A thick cathode with ≈3 mg S cm −2 loading was prepared similarly by mixing 80 wt% S-CNT composite powder, 10 wt% Super P, 5 wt% LA133 binder (Chengdu indigo Co.), and 5 wt% styrene-butadiene-rubber(SBR) binder (MTI Corp.) and forming a slurry with water.
This was coated onto a C-coated Al foil current collector (MTI Corp.).
Electrodes were punched to a 0.9 cm 2 diameter size.
The electrolytes used were either 1 M LiTFSI or 1 M LiTDI dissolved in a mixture of DOL and DME (1/1 v/v), respectively.
Nominal Li 2 S x solutions were obtained by mixing stoichiometric Li 2 S and S 8 and stirring at 60 °C in oil bath for 1–10 h inside the glove box.
The solubility was obtained by fi rst adding extra amount of stoichiometric Li 2 S 8 followed by diluting the saturated solution gradually for every 10 h until all species were dissolved.
Half cells with Li metal foil (400 μm thick from MTI Corp.) as the anode and Celgard 3501 as the separator were assembled using CR2032 coin cells in an argon-fi lled glove box.
The active S/E was carefully controlled, [ 29 ] ranging from 15 g L −1 (15 g sulfur per liter of electrolyte) to 100 g L −1 .
The discharge/charge cycles were tested galvanostatically using a Lanhe battery tester at room temperature in a voltage cutoff protocol between 2.8 and 1.5 V.
The specifi c capacity (SC) was based on the sulfur mass in the C/S composites, and the AC was calculated by the equation AC = SC × sulfur loading ratio.
Computational Details : For AIM-D simulation, the calculations were carried out with plane wave basis sets as implemented in the VASP code.

[ 38,39 ] All the calculations were spin-polarized and carried out using the gradient corrected exchange-correlation functional of PBE (Perdew, Burke, and Ernzerhof) under the projector augmented wave method, with plane wave basis set up to a kinetic energy cutoff of 300 eV.
[ 40,41 ] The van der Waals method of Grimme (i.e., DFT-D2) was used throughout AI-MD calculations with the convergence criterion of the total energy set to be within 1 × 10 −4 eV.

[ 42 ] For the simulation of the electrolyte, the simulation box (18 × 18 × 18 Å 3 ) was consisted of randomly populated 20 solvent molecules (DOL:DME = 1:1) and 5 salt molecules (i.e., LiTDI or LiTFSI) with a solvated Li 2 S 8 molecule with presumed liquid density of ≈0.96 g cm –3 .

To investigate the thermodynamic stability of the system at room temperature, all the system were thermally equilibrated at T = 300 K based on an Nose–Hoover paticles, volume, temperature (NVT) system ensemble with a time step of 1 fs, and the production run was obtained after thermal equilibration of ≈2.5 ps.
